title: Connecting our thinking with wider sector impact from the CST Conference
author: Lucy Gambier and Doug O’Brien
summary: Writing for the CELT multi-academy trust, the authors reflect on two days at the annual Confederation of School Trusts conference and what it means for trust-level leadership. They draw out keynote themes on connection and the social fabric, stewardship and collective responsibility, and the evidence for school-led trusts. A central thread is Daniel Susskind's call to teach both and test both, meaning independent thinking and effective use of AI, which they find simple to state but hard to build into curriculum and assessment. Breakout sessions on headship highlight research showing that nothing has been removed from the head's job while more has been added, along with development pathways meant to make headship achievable and attractive. Practical ideas from other trusts, such as a friction hunt to remove avoidable barriers and asking evaluation questions before, during and after delivery, are tied back to CELT's own work.
points: School trusts are framed as a means of strengthening the social fabric, so connection and belonging are treated as leadership aims rather than add-ons.
Susskind's 'teach both and test both' gives leaders a workable principle for AI: develop and assess independent thinking alongside critical use of AI tools.
Research cited on headship shows the role keeps accreting duties, so making it attractive means building capability and pathways rather than simply asking more of heads.
HEARTS Academy Trust's 'friction hunt' offers a concrete leadership practice: look for systems, resources and routines that consume time and make effective practice harder.
ImpactEd's advice to ask evaluation questions before investing, before starting, during delivery and afterwards turns strategy review into an ongoing habit.
quotes: Schools should and must play a significant role in that fabric. They bring people together, build relationships across generations and create opportunities for children to experience success, participation and belonging.

Her reflections on stewardship and collective responsibility reinforced the purpose of working together as school-led trusts: bringing schools together to improve education and strengthen their communities.
Instead, we must prepare the next generation with a back-to-basics approach, in an uncertain world, one certainty is that the basics need to be solid.

His challenge to teach both and test both offered a useful way forward: developing and assessing learners’ ability to think independently, alongside their ability to use AI effectively and critically.
Learners need knowledge and understanding to evaluate a response, recognise an error and make an informed judgement.
Anderson Quigley have completed research in this sector, capturing the challenge clearly: “We haven’t removed anything from the Head’s job. We have simply kept adding to it.
Making headship achievable and attractive requires us to develop people’s capability while creating the conditions in which they both want to and know how to lead well.
A useful takeaway was the importance of asking questions throughout the work: before investing, before starting, during delivery and afterwards.
